chapter_text:
CHAPTER 17 - MEASURES OF DISPERSION

Introduction

An average (mean, median or mode) tells us about the CENTRE of a set of data, but it hides an important feature - how SPREAD OUT the observations are around that centre. Two batsmen may have the same average score of 40 runs, yet one is steady (35, 42, 43, 40) while the other is erratic (5, 80, 2, 73). To compare them fairly we need a measure of SCATTER or VARIABILITY. The measures that describe how the data are dispersed about a central value are called MEASURES OF DISPERSION. This chapter studies four important measures - the range, the mean deviation, the variance and the standard deviation - and a relative measure, the coefficient of variation, used to compare the variability of two different data sets. Dispersion is used everywhere: a factory manager watches the variation in the length of manufactured rods, an economist studies the spread of incomes, a teacher looks at how widely marks are scattered, and a meteorologist reports the swing in daily temperatures. In each case the average is only half the story; the amount of scatter is equally important, and sometimes more so, because it measures reliability, risk and consistency. Throughout the chapter we shall work numerical examples so that each formula is seen in action on real numbers rather than in the abstract.

17.1 MEANING OF DISPERSION

Dispersion (or variability) is the extent to which the values of a variable differ from a central value, and from one another. A GOOD measure of dispersion should be: (i) rigidly defined, (ii) based on ALL the observations, (iii) easy to compute, and (iv) suitable for further algebraic treatment. Measures of dispersion are of two kinds. An ABSOLUTE measure is expressed in the same units as the data (rupees, kg, marks). A RELATIVE measure is a pure number (or percentage) independent of the units, and is therefore used to compare two series having different units or very different averages. For each absolute measure there is a corresponding relative measure (a coefficient).

17.2 THE RANGE

The RANGE is the simplest measure of dispersion. It is the DIFFERENCE between the largest (L) and the smallest (S) observation in the data:

   Range = L - S

For the data 8, 12, 20, 5, 17 the largest value is 20 and the smallest is 5, so the range = 20 - 5 = 15. The corresponding relative measure is the COEFFICIENT OF RANGE:

   Coefficient of range = (L - S) / (L + S)

For the same data, coefficient of range = (20 - 5) / (20 + 5) = 15 / 25 = 0.6. The range is quick to find and useful in quality control and weather reports, but it depends ONLY on the two extreme values and ignores how the middle values are distributed. It is also badly affected by a single unusually large or small value (an outlier). Hence the range is a crude measure.

17.3 MEAN DEVIATION

A better measure uses ALL the observations. The MEAN DEVIATION is the arithmetic mean of the ABSOLUTE deviations of the observations from a central value A (the mean or the median). We take absolute values (ignore the sign) because the ordinary signed deviations from the mean always add up to zero. For n ungrouped observations x1, x2, ..., xn,

   Mean deviation about A = (1/n) sum |xi - A|

For grouped or frequency data with frequencies f1, f2, ..., and N = sum f,

   Mean deviation about A = (1/N) sum fi |xi - A|

Worked example (about the mean): for 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, the mean xbar = 40/5 = 8. The absolute deviations |x - 8| are 4, 2, 0, 2, 4, whose sum is 12. So the mean deviation about the mean = 12/5 = 2.4.

The mean deviation may be taken about the MEDIAN instead of the mean. A useful property is that the mean deviation is LEAST when taken about the median - the sum of absolute deviations is minimum at the median. The relative measure is the COEFFICIENT OF MEAN DEVIATION = mean deviation / A (dividing by the mean or the median used). A drawback of the mean deviation is the use of absolute values, which makes it awkward for further algebra. This drawback is removed by squaring the deviations, which leads to the variance and standard deviation.

17.4 VARIANCE

The VARIANCE is the arithmetic mean of the SQUARES of the deviations of the observations from their mean. Squaring removes the sign problem and gives every deviation a positive weight. For n ungrouped observations with mean xbar,

   variance = sigma^2 = (1/n) sum (xi - xbar)^2

For frequency (discrete or grouped) data with N = sum f,

   variance = sigma^2 = (1/N) sum fi (xi - xbar)^2

Worked example: for 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 the mean xbar = 30/5 = 6. The deviations (x - 6) are -4, -2, 0, 2, 4; their squares are 16, 4, 0, 4, 16, summing to 40. So variance = 40/5 = 8. The variance is measured in the SQUARE of the units of the data (if the data are in cm, the variance is in cm^2), which is why we often prefer its square root.

17.5 STANDARD DEVIATION

The STANDARD DEVIATION (denoted sigma, the Greek letter sigma) is the POSITIVE SQUARE ROOT of the variance. It is the most important and most widely used measure of dispersion because it is based on all observations and is expressed in the SAME units as the data.

DIRECT METHOD (about the mean). First find the mean xbar, then

   sigma = sqrt( sum fi (xi - xbar)^2 / N )   (frequency data)
   sigma = sqrt( sum (xi - xbar)^2 / n )      (ungrouped data)

For the data 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 above, variance = 8, so sigma = sqrt(8) = 2.83.

MEAN-SQUARE (raw-moment) FORM. Expanding the square gives an equivalent and often quicker formula that avoids the mean at each step:

   sigma^2 = ( sum fi xi^2 / N ) - ( sum fi xi / N )^2 = mean of squares - square of mean

SHORTCUT / STEP-DEVIATION METHOD. When the values xi are large it is convenient to take deviations from an assumed mean A, and, for equally spaced class marks with common width h, to scale them: ui = (xi - A) / h. Then

   sigma = h * sqrt( sum fi ui^2 / N - ( sum fi ui / N )^2 )

This step-deviation method gives exactly the same answer with much smaller arithmetic. Worked example (frequency data, direct method): x = 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 with f = 1, 2, 3, 2, 1 and N = 9. Then sum f x = 10 + 40 + 90 + 80 + 50 = 270, so xbar = 270/9 = 30. The squared deviations (x - 30)^2 are 400, 100, 0, 100, 400; multiplied by f they give 400, 200, 0, 200, 400, summing to 1200. Hence variance = 1200/9 = 133.3 and sigma = sqrt(133.3) = 11.55.

17.6 PROPERTIES OF STANDARD DEVIATION

1. The standard deviation is always NON-NEGATIVE; it is zero only when all the observations are equal (no dispersion).
2. It is INDEPENDENT OF THE CHANGE OF ORIGIN: if a constant k is ADDED to (or subtracted from) every observation, the standard deviation is UNCHANGED, because every value and the mean shift together and the deviations (x - xbar) stay the same.
3. It DEPENDS ON THE CHANGE OF SCALE: if every observation is MULTIPLIED by a constant k, the standard deviation is multiplied by |k| (and the variance by k^2). Thus for y = k x + c, sigma_y = |k| sigma_x.
4. The standard deviation is the LEAST root-mean-square deviation - the root-mean-square deviation taken about any value A is smallest when A is the mean.
5. For the first n natural numbers, sigma = sqrt((n^2 - 1)/12).
6. COMBINED STANDARD DEVIATION. If two groups have sizes n1, n2, means xbar1, xbar2 and standard deviations sigma1, sigma2, the combined mean is xbar = (n1 xbar1 + n2 xbar2)/(n1 + n2), and the combined variance is

   sigma^2 = [ n1(sigma1^2 + d1^2) + n2(sigma2^2 + d2^2) ] / (n1 + n2)

where d1 = xbar1 - xbar and d2 = xbar2 - xbar are the deviations of the group means from the combined mean.

17.7 COEFFICIENT OF VARIATION

The standard deviation is an ABSOLUTE measure; it cannot fairly compare the variability of two series that are measured in different units or that have very different averages. For this we use a RELATIVE measure, the COEFFICIENT OF VARIATION (CV), defined as the standard deviation expressed as a PERCENTAGE of the mean:

   CV = 100 * sigma / xbar

Being a pure number (a percentage), the CV lets us compare two data sets directly. The series with the GREATER CV is MORE VARIABLE (or less consistent, less stable, less uniform); the series with the SMALLER CV is MORE CONSISTENT (more stable, more uniform). Worked example: batsman A has mean 50 and sigma 5, so CV = 100 x 5/50 = 10%. Batsman B has mean 40 and sigma 6, so CV = 100 x 6/40 = 15%. Since A's CV (10%) is smaller, A is the MORE CONSISTENT batsman, even though B might occasionally score more. Note that the CV is undefined when the mean is zero, and it is usually applied to data measured on a ratio scale with a genuine zero.

COMBINED MEAN AND VARIANCE (brief). When two or more groups are pooled, the combined mean and combined variance are found from the formulas in Section 17.6. The combined variance is NOT simply the average of the two variances - it also includes the spread of the group means about the combined mean (the terms d1^2 and d2^2), because pooling groups with different averages itself creates extra dispersion.

SUMMARY

- Dispersion measures how spread out data are about a central value; absolute measures carry the data's units, relative measures are pure numbers used for comparison.
- Range = L - S; coefficient of range = (L - S)/(L + S). Simple but uses only the two extreme values.
- Mean deviation about A = (1/N) sum f|x - A| (absolute deviations); least when taken about the median.
- Variance = sigma^2 = (1/N) sum f(x - xbar)^2 = (mean of squares) - (square of mean); measured in squared units.
- Standard deviation sigma = sqrt(variance), in the same units as the data. Direct method uses deviations from the mean; the shortcut/step-deviation method uses ui = (x - A)/h and sigma = h sqrt( sum f ui^2/N - (sum f ui/N)^2 ).
- Properties: sigma >= 0; unchanged by adding a constant (change of origin); multiplied by |k| on scaling; for y = kx + c, sigma_y = |k| sigma_x; for the first n natural numbers sigma = sqrt((n^2 - 1)/12).
- Combined variance: sigma^2 = [n1(sigma1^2 + d1^2) + n2(sigma2^2 + d2^2)]/(n1 + n2), with d1, d2 the deviations of group means from the combined mean.
- Coefficient of variation CV = 100 sigma/xbar (per cent); the smaller CV means the more consistent series, the larger CV the more variable series.

topics.name: Meaning of Dispersion and Range
topics.description: The idea of dispersion or variability about a central value; absolute versus relative measures; the range = L - S and the coefficient of range = (L - S)/(L + S) as the simplest measure of scatter.

topics.name: Mean Deviation
topics.description: Mean deviation about the mean and about the median for ungrouped and grouped data, MD = (1/N) sum f|x - A|; the use of absolute deviations, the median property (least MD), and the coefficient of mean deviation.

topics.name: Variance
topics.description: Variance as the mean of the squared deviations from the mean, sigma^2 = (1/N) sum f(x - xbar)^2 = mean of squares - square of mean; measured in squared units and forming the basis of the standard deviation.

topics.name: Standard Deviation (Direct and Shortcut Methods)
topics.description: Standard deviation sigma = sqrt(variance) for ungrouped, discrete and continuous data by the direct method and by the shortcut / step-deviation method using ui = (x - A)/h.

topics.name: Properties of Standard Deviation
topics.description: Key properties of sigma: non-negativity, independence of change of origin, dependence on change of scale (sigma_y = |k| sigma_x for y = kx + c), the natural-numbers result, and the combined standard deviation of two groups.

topics.name: Coefficient of Variation
topics.description: The relative measure CV = 100 sigma/xbar (per cent) for comparing the variability or consistency of two data sets with different units or means; smaller CV means more consistent.

learning_outcomes.description: Explain the meaning of dispersion and the difference between absolute and relative measures of dispersion, and describe the qualities of a good measure of dispersion.
Compute the range and the coefficient of range for ungrouped and grouped data and state the merits and limitations of the range.
Calculate the mean deviation about the mean and about the median for ungrouped and grouped data and the coefficient of mean deviation.
Define and compute the variance of ungrouped and frequency data using sigma^2 = (1/N) sum f(x - xbar)^2 and the mean-of-squares minus square-of-mean form.
Compute the standard deviation of ungrouped and discrete data by the direct method sigma = sqrt(sum f(x - xbar)^2 / N).
Compute the standard deviation of grouped/continuous data by the shortcut and step-deviation methods using ui = (x - A)/h.
State and use the properties of standard deviation, including independence of change of origin, dependence on change of scale, and the combined standard deviation of two groups.
Compute the coefficient of variation CV = 100 sigma/xbar and use it to compare the variability and consistency of two data sets.

chapter_summary.title: Measures of Dispersion - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Senior Secondary Mathematics summary covers measures of dispersion: the meaning of variability, the range and coefficient of range, the mean deviation, the variance and standard deviation (direct and shortcut methods) with their properties, and the coefficient of variation for comparing variability.

details: Simple; uses only the two extremes

sections.heading: Meaning of dispersion and the range
bullets: Dispersion measures how the observations scatter about a central value; an average alone cannot show this.
Absolute measures carry the units of the data; relative measures (coefficients) are pure numbers used to compare series.
Range = L - S is the simplest measure; coefficient of range = (L - S)/(L + S).
The range uses only the two extreme values, so it ignores the middle data and is sensitive to outliers.

sections.heading: Mean deviation
bullets: Mean deviation about A = (1/N) sum f|x - A|, the mean of the absolute deviations from the mean or median.
Absolute values are used because the signed deviations from the mean always sum to zero.
The mean deviation is least when taken about the median.
Coefficient of mean deviation = mean deviation / A.

sections.heading: Variance and standard deviation
bullets: Variance sigma^2 = (1/N) sum f(x - xbar)^2 is the mean of the squared deviations, in squared units.
Equivalent form: variance = (sum f x^2 / N) - (sum f x / N)^2 = mean of squares - square of mean.
Standard deviation sigma = sqrt(variance) is in the same units as the data and is the most widely used measure.
Shortcut/step-deviation method: ui = (x - A)/h and sigma = h sqrt(sum f ui^2/N - (sum f ui/N)^2).

sections.heading: Properties of standard deviation
bullets: sigma is never negative and is zero only when all observations are equal.
Adding a constant to every value leaves sigma unchanged (independent of change of origin).
Multiplying every value by k multiplies sigma by |k|; for y = kx + c, sigma_y = |k| sigma_x.
Combined variance = [n1(sigma1^2 + d1^2) + n2(sigma2^2 + d2^2)]/(n1 + n2).

sections.heading: Coefficient of variation
bullets: CV = 100 sigma/xbar expresses the standard deviation as a percentage of the mean.
As a pure number, CV compares data sets with different units or different averages.
The series with the smaller CV is more consistent/stable; the larger CV is more variable.
CV is undefined when the mean is zero.

key_takeaways: Dispersion describes the scatter of data about a central value; absolute measures carry units, relative measures are pure numbers.
Range = L - S and coefficient of range = (L - S)/(L + S) are quick but depend only on the extreme values.
Mean deviation = (1/N) sum f|x - A| uses absolute deviations and is least about the median.
Variance sigma^2 = (1/N) sum f(x - xbar)^2 = mean of squares - square of mean; standard deviation sigma = sqrt(variance).
The step-deviation method sigma = h sqrt(sum f u^2/N - (sum f u/N)^2) simplifies the arithmetic for grouped data.
sigma is unchanged by adding a constant and multiplied by |k| on scaling; combined variance adds the spread of group means.
CV = 100 sigma/xbar; the smaller CV marks the more consistent series.

glossary.definition: The extent to which the observations of a data set differ from a central value and from one another; also called variability or scatter.
A measure of scatter expressed in the same units as the data, such as the range, mean deviation or standard deviation.
A unit-free measure (a coefficient or percentage) used to compare the variability of two data sets, such as the coefficient of variation.
The difference between the largest and smallest observations, Range = L - S; the simplest measure of dispersion.
The relative measure of the range, equal to (L - S)/(L + S), a pure number.
The arithmetic mean of the absolute deviations of the observations from a central value A, MD = (1/N) sum f|x - A|.
The relative measure of the mean deviation, equal to (mean deviation)/A where A is the mean or median used.
The mean of the squared deviations from the mean, sigma^2 = (1/N) sum f(x - xbar)^2; measured in squared units.
The positive square root of the variance, sigma = sqrt(variance); in the same units as the data and the most used measure of dispersion.
A shortcut for standard deviation using ui = (x - A)/h, giving sigma = h sqrt(sum f u^2/N - (sum f u/N)^2).
Adding or subtracting a constant to every observation; it leaves the standard deviation unchanged.
Multiplying every observation by a constant k; it multiplies the standard deviation by |k| and the variance by k^2.
The variance of two pooled groups, [n1(sigma1^2 + d1^2) + n2(sigma2^2 + d2^2)]/(n1 + n2), with d the deviation of a group mean from the combined mean.
The relative measure CV = 100 sigma/xbar, expressing the standard deviation as a percentage of the mean; used to compare variability.
An unusually large or small observation that strongly affects crude measures such as the range.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Measures of Dispersion (NIOS Senior Secondary Mathematics)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Show full working for numerical problems. Give standard deviations correct to two decimal places and coefficients of variation as percentages.

questions.question: Define dispersion. Distinguish between an absolute and a relative measure of dispersion, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: Dispersion is the extent to which the observations of a data set differ from a central value and from one another (its variability or scatter). An ABSOLUTE measure of dispersion is expressed in the same units as the data - for example the standard deviation (in kg, marks, rupees). A RELATIVE measure is a pure number, independent of the units, obtained by dividing an absolute measure by an average - for example the coefficient of variation CV = 100 sigma/xbar. Relative measures are used to compare two series that have different units or very different averages.
questions.explanation: Meaning + absolute (units) vs relative (pure number) with examples.

questions.question: Find the range and the coefficient of range for the data: 25, 18, 32, 40, 15, 28.
questions.answer:
The largest value is L = 40 and the smallest is S = 15.

Range = L - S = 40 - 15 = 25.

Coefficient of range = (L - S)/(L + S) = (40 - 15)/(40 + 15) = 25/55 = 0.4545, i.e. about 0.45.
questions.explanation: Range = 40 - 15 = 25; coefficient = 25/55 = 0.45.

questions.question: Calculate the mean deviation about the mean for the data: 6, 8, 10, 12, 14.
questions.answer:
Mean xbar = (6 + 8 + 10 + 12 + 14)/5 = 50/5 = 10.

Absolute deviations |x - 10|: 4, 2, 0, 2, 4. Their sum = 12.

Mean deviation about the mean = (1/n) sum |x - xbar| = 12/5 = 2.4.

questions.question: Compute the variance of the observations 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.
questions.explanation: xbar = 6; sum of squared deviations = 40; variance = 8.

questions.question: Find the standard deviation of 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 by the direct method.
questions.explanation: xbar = 15; sum sq dev = 250; variance 50; sigma = sqrt(50) = 7.07.

questions.question: For the frequency distribution x = 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 with frequencies f = 2, 4, 6, 4, 2, compute the mean and the standard deviation by the direct method.
questions.explanation: N = 18; xbar = 30; sum f(x-xbar)^2 = 2400; variance 133.33; sigma = 11.55.

questions.question: The standard deviation of a set of marks is 8. If 5 marks are added to every student's score, what is the new standard deviation? Justify.
questions.answer:
Adding a constant to every observation is a change of ORIGIN, which does not change the standard deviation. Every value and the mean shift up by 5, so the deviations (x - xbar) are unchanged and hence so is sigma.

New standard deviation = 8 (unchanged).
questions.explanation: Change of origin leaves sigma unchanged; still 8.

questions.question: Two workers' daily outputs have the following statistics: Worker A - mean 50 units, standard deviation 5 units; Worker B - mean 40 units, standard deviation 6 units. Find the coefficient of variation of each and state who is more consistent.
questions.answer:
Coefficient of variation CV = 100 sigma / xbar.

Worker A: CV = 100 x 5 / 50 = 10%.
Worker B: CV = 100 x 6 / 40 = 15%.

The smaller coefficient of variation indicates the more consistent (more uniform) worker. Since A's CV (10%) is less than B's CV (15%), Worker A is MORE CONSISTENT in daily output, even though comparing standard deviations alone (5 vs 6) is misleading because the two means differ.
questions.explanation: CV_A = 10%, CV_B = 15%; smaller CV => A more consistent.

questions.question: Using the step-deviation method with assumed mean A = 30 and class width h = 10, find the standard deviation of x = 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 with frequencies f = 1, 2, 3, 2, 1.

Two groups have the following data: Group 1 has 40 items with mean 20 and standard deviation 3; Group 2 has 60 items with mean 25 and standard deviation 4. Find the combined mean and the combined standard deviation.
questions.explanation: Combined mean 23; d1=-3, d2=2; combined variance 19.2; sigma = 4.38.

questions.question: A measure of dispersion expressed as a pure number is called a ____ measure.
questions.explanation: Relative measures are unit-free.

questions.question: Measures of dispersion describe the ____ of the data about a central value.
questions.explanation: Also called scatter or variability.

questions.question: The range of a data set equals L - ____ .
questions.explanation: Range = largest - smallest.

questions.explanation: Relative measure of the range.

questions.explanation: Least sum of absolute deviations.

questions.question: The variance is the mean of the ____ deviations from the mean.
questions.explanation: sigma^2 = (1/N) sum (x - xbar)^2.

questions.explanation: sigma^2 = sum x^2/n - (sum x/n)^2.

questions.explanation: h is the class width.

questions.question: In the step-deviation method sigma = h sqrt(sum f u^2/N - (sum f u/____)^2).
questions.explanation: The bracket is the mean of u.

questions.question: For y = kx + c, the standard deviation of y equals ____ times the SD of x.
questions.explanation: SD depends on scale, not on the added constant.

questions.question: For the first n natural numbers, sigma = sqrt((n^2 - 1)/ ____ ).
questions.explanation: Standard result.

questions.question: The coefficient of variation equals 100 x sigma / ____ .
questions.explanation: CV = 100 sigma/mean.

questions.question: What is meant by dispersion? Why is a measure of central tendency alone not enough to describe data?
questions.answer: Dispersion is the extent to which the observations differ from a central value and from one another - the scatter or variability of the data. A measure of central tendency such as the mean tells us only about the CENTRE of the data; it cannot show whether the values are tightly clustered or widely spread. Two data sets can share the same mean yet have very different spreads, so a measure of dispersion is needed to describe the data fully.
questions.explanation: Dispersion = scatter; averages miss the spread.

questions.question: List any three qualities of a good measure of dispersion.
questions.answer: A good measure of dispersion should be: (1) rigidly (clearly) defined so that it has a single value for a given data set; (2) based on ALL the observations, not just a few; (3) easy to understand and compute; and (4) suitable for further algebraic/mathematical treatment. It should also not be affected unduly by a single extreme value. (Any three.)
questions.explanation: Rigidly defined, based on all data, easy, algebraically tractable.

questions.question: Find the range and coefficient of range for 45, 30, 55, 20, 60.
questions.answer:
L = 60, S = 20.
Range = L - S = 60 - 20 = 40.
Coefficient of range = (L - S)/(L + S) = 40/80 = 0.5.
questions.explanation: Range 40; coefficient 40/80 = 0.5.

questions.question: State two merits and two limitations of the range as a measure of dispersion.
questions.answer:
Merits: (1) it is the simplest measure of dispersion and very easy to calculate; (2) it gives a quick idea of the spread and is useful in quality control and weather reports.
Limitations: (1) it is based only on the two extreme values and ignores how the middle observations are distributed; (2) it is badly affected by a single unusually large or small value (an outlier), so it is not a reliable measure.
questions.explanation: Merits: simple, quick. Limitations: only extremes, outlier-sensitive.

questions.question: The maximum and minimum daily temperatures in a week were 38 C and 26 C. Find the coefficient of range.
Calculate the mean deviation about the mean for 10, 20, 30, 40, 50.
questions.answer:
Mean xbar = 150/5 = 30.
Absolute deviations |x - 30|: 20, 10, 0, 10, 20; sum = 60.
Mean deviation about mean = 60/5 = 12.

questions.question: Find the mean deviation about the median for the data 4, 7, 8, 9, 12.
questions.answer:
Arranged in order the data are 4, 7, 8, 9, 12; the median (middle value) is 8.
Absolute deviations |x - 8|: 4, 1, 0, 1, 4; sum = 10.
Mean deviation about the median = 10/5 = 2.
questions.explanation: Median 8; sum|x-8| = 10; MD = 2.

questions.question: Why are absolute values used when computing the mean deviation?
questions.answer: The ordinary (signed) deviations of observations from their mean always add up to zero, because the positive and negative deviations cancel: sum(x - xbar) = 0. If we simply averaged the signed deviations we would always get zero, which tells us nothing about the spread. Taking ABSOLUTE values removes the signs so that all deviations count as positive contributions to the scatter, giving a meaningful measure.
questions.explanation: Signed deviations sum to zero; |.| keeps them positive.

questions.question: Compute the variance of 3, 6, 9, 12, 15.
questions.answer:
Mean xbar = 45/5 = 9.
Deviations (x - 9): -6, -3, 0, 3, 6; squares: 36, 9, 0, 9, 36; sum = 90.
Variance = 90/5 = 18.
questions.explanation: xbar = 9; sum sq dev = 90; variance = 18.

questions.question: Using the identity variance = mean of squares - square of mean, find the variance of 2, 4, 6, 8.
questions.answer:
Mean xbar = 20/4 = 5, so square of mean = 25.
Squares: 4, 16, 36, 64; sum = 120; mean of squares = 120/4 = 30.
Variance = 30 - 25 = 5.
questions.explanation: Mean of squares 30; square of mean 25; variance 5.

questions.question: State the formula for the variance of a frequency distribution and name each symbol.
questions.answer: For a frequency distribution the variance is sigma^2 = (1/N) sum f(x - xbar)^2, where x is the value (or class mark), f is the corresponding frequency, N = sum f is the total frequency, and xbar = (sum f x)/N is the mean. It is the frequency-weighted mean of the squared deviations from the mean.
questions.explanation: sigma^2 = (1/N) sum f(x - xbar)^2 with x, f, N, xbar defined.

questions.question: Find the standard deviation of 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 by the direct method.
questions.answer:
Mean xbar = 60/5 = 12.
Deviations (x - 12): -8, -4, 0, 4, 8; squares: 64, 16, 0, 16, 64; sum = 160.
Variance = 160/5 = 32, so sigma = sqrt(32) = 5.66.
questions.explanation: xbar = 12; sum sq dev = 160; variance 32; sigma = 5.66.

questions.question: The runs scored by a batsman in five innings are 30, 40, 50, 60, 70. Find the standard deviation.
questions.explanation: xbar = 50; sum sq dev = 1000; variance 200; sigma = 14.14.

questions.question: Find the standard deviation of the first five natural numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
questions.answer:
Mean xbar = 15/5 = 3.
Deviations (x - 3): -2, -1, 0, 1, 2; squares: 4, 1, 0, 1, 4; sum = 10.
Variance = 10/5 = 2, so sigma = sqrt(2) = 1.41.
(Check: sqrt((n^2 - 1)/12) = sqrt(24/12) = sqrt(2).)
questions.explanation: xbar = 3; variance 2; sigma = sqrt(2) = 1.41.

questions.question: Using an assumed mean A = 25 for the data 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, find the standard deviation by the deviation method (h = 1).
questions.answer:
Take d = x - 25: -10, -5, 0, 5, 10 (here h = 1 so u = d).
sum d = 0, so mean of d = 0.
d^2: 100, 25, 0, 25, 100; sum d^2 = 250; mean of d^2 = 250/5 = 50.
sigma = sqrt(mean of d^2 - (mean of d)^2) = sqrt(50 - 0) = 7.07.
questions.explanation: d = x-25; sum d = 0; sum d^2 = 250; sigma = sqrt(50) = 7.07.

questions.question: For classes with mid-values 5, 15, 25, 35, 45 and frequencies 2, 3, 5, 3, 2 (N = 15), use A = 25, h = 10 to find sum f u and sum f u^2.
Why does the step-deviation method give the same standard deviation as the direct method?
questions.answer: The step deviation u = (x - A)/h is obtained from x by subtracting a constant A (a change of origin) and dividing by a constant h (a change of scale). Subtracting A does not affect the standard deviation, and dividing by h divides the standard deviation by h. So sigma_x = h x sigma_u. The method only rescales the arithmetic; when we multiply back by h we recover exactly the same standard deviation as the direct method.
questions.explanation: u shifts origin (no effect) and scales by 1/h; multiplying by h restores sigma.

questions.question: State the effect on the standard deviation of (a) adding a constant to every observation and (b) multiplying every observation by a constant k.
questions.answer:
(a) Adding (or subtracting) a constant to every observation is a change of ORIGIN. Every value and the mean shift by the same amount, so the deviations (x - xbar) are unchanged and the standard deviation is UNCHANGED.
(b) Multiplying every observation by a constant k is a change of SCALE. Each deviation is multiplied by k, so the standard deviation is multiplied by |k| (and the variance by k^2). In general, for y = kx + c, sigma_y = |k| sigma_x.
questions.explanation: Origin: no change. Scale: sigma multiplied by |k|.

questions.question: Two samples: n1 = 5, xbar1 = 10; n2 = 5, xbar2 = 20. Both have SD 2. Find the combined mean and combined variance.
questions.explanation: Combined mean 15; d = ±5; combined variance 29.

questions.question: The mean of a data set is 25 and its standard deviation is 5. Find the coefficient of variation.
Two brands of bulbs have lifetimes: Brand X mean 1000 h, SD 100 h; Brand Y mean 1200 h, SD 150 h. Which brand is more consistent?
questions.answer:
CV(X) = 100 x 100/1000 = 10%.
CV(Y) = 100 x 150/1200 = 12.5%.
Brand X has the smaller coefficient of variation (10% < 12.5%), so Brand X is MORE CONSISTENT (its lifetimes are relatively less variable), even though Brand Y lasts longer on average.
questions.explanation: CV_X = 10%, CV_Y = 12.5%; X more consistent.

questions.question: Why is the coefficient of variation preferred over the standard deviation when comparing two different data sets?
questions.answer: The standard deviation is an ABSOLUTE measure carrying the units of the data, so it cannot fairly compare series measured in different units or having very different averages - a large SD may just reflect a large mean. The coefficient of variation CV = 100 sigma/xbar is a RELATIVE, unit-free measure that expresses the SD as a percentage of the mean. Being a pure number it allows a direct comparison of variability, and the series with the smaller CV is the more consistent.
questions.explanation: CV is unit-free and mean-relative, so it compares fairly.

questions.question: Explain the meaning of dispersion and distinguish clearly between absolute and relative measures of dispersion, naming the common measures of each type.
questions.answer:
Dispersion (variability or scatter) is the degree to which the observations of a data set differ from a central value and from one another. It answers the question: are the values tightly bunched around the average or widely spread out? Two data sets with the same average can differ greatly in their scatter, so dispersion is an essential complement to an average.

Measures of dispersion are of two kinds.
ABSOLUTE measures are expressed in the SAME units as the data (rupees, kg, marks). The common absolute measures are the range, the mean deviation, and the standard deviation (with the variance). Because they carry units, two absolute measures can be compared only if the data are in the same units and have comparable averages.
RELATIVE measures are PURE NUMBERS (often percentages) obtained by dividing an absolute measure by an appropriate average. For each absolute measure there is a matching relative one: coefficient of range = (L - S)/(L + S), coefficient of mean deviation = MD/A, and coefficient of variation = 100 sigma/xbar. Because they are unit-free, relative measures let us compare the variability of series with different units or very different means.

In short, an absolute measure tells us HOW MUCH the data scatter in the original units, while a relative measure tells us how large that scatter is RELATIVE to the size of the data, enabling fair comparison.
questions.explanation: Dispersion defined; absolute (units) vs relative (pure number) with the standard examples.

questions.question: For the data 12, 25, 33, 18, 42, 27 find the range and the coefficient of range, and explain why the range is called a crude measure of dispersion.
questions.answer:
Arranged: 12, 18, 25, 27, 33, 42. Largest L = 42, smallest S = 12.

Range = L - S = 42 - 12 = 30.
Coefficient of range = (L - S)/(L + S) = 30/54 = 0.556, i.e. about 0.56.

The range is called a crude measure because it uses ONLY the two extreme observations (42 and 12) and takes no account of how the remaining values are distributed between them. If the middle values changed completely, the range would stay 30 as long as the extremes were unchanged. It is also very sensitive to an outlier: a single unusually large or small value would swing the range sharply. Because it is not based on all the observations, the range gives only a rough idea of dispersion.
questions.explanation: Range 30; coefficient 30/54 = 0.56; crude because only extremes used.

questions.question: Calculate the mean deviation about the mean for the frequency distribution x = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 with frequencies f = 1, 2, 3, 2, 2.
questions.explanation: N = 10; xbar = 6.4; sum f|x-xbar| = 20.8; MD = 2.08.

questions.question: For 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 find the variance both by the direct method and by the mean-of-squares minus square-of-mean method, and confirm they agree.
questions.answer:
Mean xbar = 45/5 = 9.

Direct method: deviations (x - 9): -4, -2, 0, 2, 4; squares: 16, 4, 0, 4, 16; sum = 40. Variance = 40/5 = 8.

Mean-of-squares method: squares of x are 25, 49, 81, 121, 169; sum = 445; mean of squares = 445/5 = 89. Square of mean = 9^2 = 81.
Variance = 89 - 81 = 8.

Both methods give variance = 8, so sigma = sqrt(8) = 2.83. The two approaches agree, as they must, since expanding (x - xbar)^2 leads exactly to (mean of squares) - (square of mean).
questions.explanation: Direct: 40/5 = 8. Mean-of-squares: 89 - 81 = 8. Both = 8.

questions.question: The heights (cm) of 5 plants are 20, 22, 24, 26, 28. Find the mean, variance and standard deviation, and state the units of each.
questions.answer:
Mean xbar = (20 + 22 + 24 + 26 + 28)/5 = 120/5 = 24 cm.

Deviations (x - 24): -4, -2, 0, 2, 4; squares: 16, 4, 0, 4, 16; sum = 40.

Variance sigma^2 = 40/5 = 8 cm^2 (note the SQUARED units).

Standard deviation sigma = sqrt(8) = 2.83 cm (same units as the data).

So the mean height is 24 cm, the variance is 8 cm^2, and the standard deviation is about 2.83 cm - the heights typically lie within about 2.83 cm of the mean.
questions.explanation: xbar = 24 cm; variance 8 cm^2; sigma = 2.83 cm.

questions.question: The following table gives the marks of 20 students in classes with mid-values x = 5, 15, 25, 35, 45 and frequencies f = 2, 3, 8, 5, 2. Using assumed mean A = 25 and h = 10, find the mean and standard deviation by the step-deviation method.
questions.explanation: sum fu = 2, sum fu^2 = 24; mean 26; sigma = 10 sqrt(1.19) = 10.91.

questions.question: State the change-of-origin and change-of-scale properties of the standard deviation. Then, given that 20, 40, 60, 80, 100 has SD 28.28, find the SD of (a) 25, 45, 65, 85, 105 and (b) 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, without full recomputation.
questions.answer:
Properties: (i) Change of origin - adding or subtracting a constant to every value leaves the standard deviation UNCHANGED. (ii) Change of scale - multiplying every value by k multiplies the standard deviation by |k|; in general for y = kx + c, sigma_y = |k| sigma_x.

The original data 20, 40, 60, 80, 100 have SD 28.28.

(a) 25, 45, 65, 85, 105 is obtained by adding 5 to every value (change of origin only). So the SD is UNCHANGED: SD = 28.28.

(b) 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 is obtained by multiplying every value by k = 1/2 (change of scale). So SD = |1/2| x 28.28 = 14.14.

Thus the properties let us write down the new standard deviations without redoing the full calculation.
questions.explanation: Origin: SD unchanged (28.28). Scale by 1/2: SD = 14.14.

questions.question: The scores of two students in five tests are: Student A - 45, 50, 55, 50, 50; Student B - 30, 70, 40, 60, 50. Compute the mean, standard deviation and coefficient of variation of each, and decide who is more consistent.
questions.answer:
Student A: mean = (45 + 50 + 55 + 50 + 50)/5 = 250/5 = 50.
Deviations: -5, 0, 5, 0, 0; squares: 25, 0, 25, 0, 0; sum = 50; variance = 50/5 = 10; sigma_A = sqrt(10) = 3.16.
CV(A) = 100 x 3.16/50 = 6.32%.

Student B: mean = (30 + 70 + 40 + 60 + 50)/5 = 250/5 = 50.
Deviations: -20, 20, -10, 10, 0; squares: 400, 400, 100, 100, 0; sum = 1000; variance = 1000/5 = 200; sigma_B = sqrt(200) = 14.14.
CV(B) = 100 x 14.14/50 = 28.28%.

Both have the same mean (50), but CV(A) = 6.32% is far smaller than CV(B) = 28.28%. Therefore Student A is MUCH MORE CONSISTENT; Student B's scores are far more variable.
questions.explanation: A: sigma 3.16, CV 6.32%. B: sigma 14.14, CV 28.28%. A more consistent.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Measures of dispersion tell us how the observations scatter about a central value. They are of two kinds: absolute measures, expressed in the units of the data, and relative measures, which are pure numbers. A teacher records the marks of two classes with the same average of 60, but Class P ranges from 55 to 65 while Class Q ranges from 30 to 90.
(a) Which class shows greater dispersion?
(b) Name one absolute and one relative measure of dispersion.
(c) Why can two classes have the same mean yet differ in dispersion?
(d) Which type of measure would you use to compare classes with different average marks?
questions.answer:
(a) Class Q shows greater dispersion, since its marks are spread over a much wider interval (30 to 90) than Class P (55 to 65).
(b) Absolute measure: standard deviation (or range/mean deviation). Relative measure: coefficient of variation (or coefficient of range).
(c) The mean fixes only the CENTRE of the data; the observations can be clustered tightly or spread widely about that centre, so equal means can accompany very different spreads.
(d) A relative measure such as the coefficient of variation, because it is unit-free and expresses spread relative to the mean, allowing fair comparison across different averages.
questions.explanation: Q more spread; SD absolute, CV relative; mean fixes centre only; use CV.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The range is the simplest measure of dispersion: Range = L - S, with coefficient of range = (L - S)/(L + S). The weekly wages (in rupees) of six workers are 200, 250, 300, 180, 420, 260.
(a) Identify L and S.
(b) Find the range.
(c) Find the coefficient of range.
(d) State one limitation of the range shown by this data.
questions.answer:
(a) L = 420 (largest) and S = 180 (smallest).
(b) Range = L - S = 420 - 180 = 240.
(c) Coefficient of range = (420 - 180)/(420 + 180) = 240/600 = 0.4.
(d) The range (240) is fixed entirely by the two extreme wages 420 and 180 and ignores the four middle wages; a single high wage (420) inflates it, so it gives only a rough picture of the spread.
questions.explanation: L = 420, S = 180; range 240; coefficient 0.4; only extremes used.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The mean deviation about a central value A is MD = (1/n) sum |x - A|. Consider the data 5, 9, 11, 13, 17.
(a) Find the mean.
(b) Compute the mean deviation about the mean.
(c) The median is 11. Compute the mean deviation about the median.
(d) Which of the two mean deviations is smaller, and is that expected?
questions.answer:
(a) Mean xbar = (5 + 9 + 11 + 13 + 17)/5 = 55/5 = 11.
(b) |x - 11|: 6, 2, 0, 2, 6; sum = 16; MD about mean = 16/5 = 3.2.
(c) The median is also 11 here, so |x - 11| gives the same values 6, 2, 0, 2, 6; sum = 16; MD about median = 16/5 = 3.2.
(d) They are equal (3.2) because the mean and median coincide for this symmetric data. In general the mean deviation about the median is the smaller (least) one, as expected from the median property.
questions.explanation: Mean 11; MD about mean 3.2; median 11; equal here; median MD is least in general.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The variance is sigma^2 = (1/n) sum (x - xbar)^2 and can also be found as mean of squares minus square of mean. Take the data 4, 6, 8, 10, 12.
(a) Find the mean.
(b) Find the variance by the direct method.
(c) Verify it using mean of squares minus square of mean.
(d) What are the units of the variance if the data are in cm?
questions.answer:
(a) Mean xbar = 40/5 = 8.
(b) Deviations: -4, -2, 0, 2, 4; squares: 16, 4, 0, 4, 16; sum = 40; variance = 40/5 = 8.
(c) Squares of x: 16, 36, 64, 100, 144; sum = 360; mean of squares = 360/5 = 72; square of mean = 64; variance = 72 - 64 = 8. This matches (b).
(d) The variance would be in cm^2 (the squared units), since squaring the deviations squares the units.
questions.explanation: Mean 8; variance 8 both ways; units cm^2.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The standard deviation sigma = sqrt(variance) is the most used measure of dispersion. A machine produces rods whose lengths (cm) in a sample are 48, 50, 52, 50, 50.
(a) Find the mean length.
(b) Find the variance.
(c) Find the standard deviation.
(d) State one reason the standard deviation is preferred over the range.
questions.answer:
(a) Mean xbar = (48 + 50 + 52 + 50 + 50)/5 = 250/5 = 50 cm.
(b) Deviations: -2, 0, 2, 0, 0; squares: 4, 0, 4, 0, 0; sum = 8; variance = 8/5 = 1.6 cm^2.
(c) sigma = sqrt(1.6) = 1.26 cm.
(d) The standard deviation is based on ALL the observations and is suitable for further algebraic work, whereas the range uses only the two extreme values and is easily distorted by an outlier.
questions.explanation: Mean 50; variance 1.6; sigma = 1.26; SD uses all data.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
For grouped data the step-deviation method uses u = (x - A)/h and sigma = h sqrt(sum f u^2/N - (sum f u/N)^2). A distribution has mid-values x = 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 with frequencies f = 4, 6, 10, 6, 4 (N = 30). Take A = 30, h = 10.
(a) Write the u-values.
(b) Find sum f u and sum f u^2.
(c) Find the mean.
(d) Find the standard deviation.
questions.explanation: u = (x-30)/10; sum fu = 0, sum fu^2 = 44; mean 30; sigma = 12.11.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The standard deviation is unchanged by a change of origin but is multiplied by |k| on a change of scale (for y = kx + c, sigma_y = |k| sigma_x). A data set has standard deviation 6.
(a) Find the new SD if 10 is added to every value.
(b) Find the new SD if every value is multiplied by 4.
(c) Find the new SD for the transformation y = 3x + 7.
(d) What happens to the variance when every value is multiplied by 4?
questions.answer:
(a) Adding 10 is a change of origin, so the SD is unchanged: 6.
(b) Multiplying by 4 is a change of scale: new SD = 4 x 6 = 24.
(c) For y = 3x + 7, sigma_y = |3| x 6 = 18 (the +7 has no effect).
(d) Multiplying every value by 4 multiplies the variance by 4^2 = 16, so the new variance = 16 x 36 = 576 (since original variance = 6^2 = 36).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The coefficient of variation CV = 100 sigma/xbar compares the variability of data sets. In a factory, the daily production of two machines gave: Machine I - mean 200 units, SD 20 units; Machine II - mean 250 units, SD 20 units.
(a) Find the CV of Machine I.
(b) Find the CV of Machine II.
(c) Which machine is more consistent?
(d) Why is comparing the SDs (both 20) alone misleading here?
questions.answer:
(a) CV(I) = 100 x 20/200 = 10%.
(b) CV(II) = 100 x 20/250 = 8%.
(c) Machine II has the smaller CV (8% < 10%), so Machine II is MORE CONSISTENT.
(d) Both machines have the same SD (20 units), which suggests equal variability, but they have different means. Relative to its higher mean (250), Machine II's spread is proportionally smaller, so the SDs alone hide the true difference; the CV, being relative, reveals it.
questions.explanation: CV_I = 10%, CV_II = 8%; II more consistent; equal SD misleads with different means.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Two cricketers' scores in six matches are: Player A - 40, 50, 60, 40, 50, 60; Player B - 10, 90, 40, 60, 20, 80. Both have the same mean.
(a) Verify the mean of each is 50.
(b) Find the SD of Player A (variance = 66.67).
(c) Find the SD of Player B (variance = 866.67).
(d) Using the coefficient of variation, state who is the more consistent player.
questions.answer:
(a) A: (40+50+60+40+50+60)/6 = 300/6 = 50. B: (10+90+40+60+20+80)/6 = 300/6 = 50. Both means are 50.
(b) sigma_A = sqrt(66.67) = 8.16.
(c) sigma_B = sqrt(866.67) = 29.44.
(d) CV(A) = 100 x 8.16/50 = 16.33%; CV(B) = 100 x 29.44/50 = 58.88%. Since CV(A) is far smaller, Player A is much MORE CONSISTENT; Player B's scores swing widely.
questions.explanation: Mean 50 each; sigma_A 8.16, sigma_B 29.44; CV_A 16.3% < CV_B 58.9%; A more consistent.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The standard deviation sigma = sqrt(variance) measures scatter in the same units as the data. The daily maximum temperatures (C) over five days were 30, 32, 34, 36, 38.
(a) Find the mean temperature.
(b) Find the variance.
(c) Find the standard deviation.
(d) If every reading rose by 2 C, what would the new standard deviation be?
questions.answer:
(a) Mean xbar = (30 + 32 + 34 + 36 + 38)/5 = 170/5 = 34 C.
(b) Deviations (x - 34): -4, -2, 0, 2, 4; squares: 16, 4, 0, 4, 16; sum = 40; variance = 40/5 = 8.
(c) sigma = sqrt(8) = 2.83 C.
(d) Adding 2 to every reading is a change of origin, so the standard deviation is UNCHANGED: 2.83 C.
questions.explanation: Mean 34; variance 8; sigma = 2.83; adding 2 leaves SD unchanged.
